prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B005 alone, with Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye, and I do not change my configuration from round 1. The chair asks what the magic-wavelength lattice adds beyond the 2005 comb and the 2012 ion-control prizes. My answer, as a theorist, is that the comb supplied the ruler and Wineland-type control supplied a single, almost perfectly isolated quantum absorber. The lattice clock solved a different problem: by choosing the trap wavelength so that both clock levels shift equally, it removes motional and light-shift errors for a large ensemble at once. This turns the clock from a one-ion device limited by its signal-to-noise into a many-body system with enough statistics to reach about 1e-18 in hours, and it is the reason the gravitational redshift can be resolved across millimetres. That is a conceptual step (an engineered cancellation of a systematic effect for N atoms) and not only averaging, since without the magic condition averaging many atoms would only average many shifts. Kroll and Lindroth describe the same mechanism, and the quantitative agreement between calculated magic wavelengths, blackbody shifts and measured clock frequencies is the kind of reproducible theory-experiment closure I value most. The result has been reproduced independently at several institutes and compared over fibre links, so maturity does not depend on waiting for the formal redefinition of the SI second. I read that redefinition as a consequence of the clock's performance, and a prize now would not be premature. I propose a narrow citation tied to the lattice clock, not to the comb or to metrology in general.
statement.case_against: The reservations remain real. A sceptic can call the lattice clock an extremely successful refinement of a lineage already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and a measurement advance is not the same as finding a new state of matter or a new particle. Only tightened bounds on varying constants and dark-matter couplings have been obtained so far, so the strongest physical payoff is still prospective. Two names cannot carry the contributions of Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Derevianko and the ion-clock groups, and I cannot settle the priority chronology between Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and parallel lattice ideas from the supplied text. Atomic physics is outside my core field, so I rely on Lindroth and Kroll for the judgement that the lattice step is large enough. If the committee wants a second part with a new quantum state at its centre, B014 is the natural candidate, but I still see unresolved credit for the experimental groups and an unsettled pairing mechanism, so I do not add it to my configuration.

responses.point: He states that the lattice-clock concept is distinct from both prior prizes, since Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes the light shift so thousands of atoms can be interrogated, and that Ye's group then showed real averaging power; he weighs the overlap and the SI redefinition as real but not decisive.
responses.response: I accept this and it answers the question I put to Lindroth in round 1. Your point that the many-atom approach gives real averaging power is correct, but I would add that it is only available because of the magic condition, which is why I regard the step as conceptual and not as mere averaging. Your Boulder year in Hall's laboratory makes you well placed to judge the comb lineage, and I take your view that the overlap is not decisive. Where I would be more careful than your summary is the credit: I would not wait for the redefinition, but I would ask outside experts to check the first strontium lattice-clock measurements against Katori's proposal before we fix the pair.

responses.point: He argues that the clock is a clue from nature in his sense, because 1e-18 clocks test constants, ultralight dark matter and gravitational redshift, but he also notes that no variation or violation has been found, so the result is a tightened bound and a quieter story.
responses.response: I agree with both halves. The redshift measurement over millimetres is a laboratory test of general relativity that was out of reach before, and it qualifies the work as discovery-enabling. I also accept that a null result is a quieter story. I would not make a measured violation a condition of the prize, since the Nobel mandate has never required that the effect found be the one expected, and the committee should not hold precision work to a stricter standard than other fields. On your concern about the timing, I read the pending redefinition of the second as supporting a prize now.

responses.point: She finds the case persuasive because magic wavelengths and blackbody shifts are a place where atomic many-body calculation and measurement meet at exceptional precision, and she keeps B015 or B014 as the answer if the committee wants a clearly new discovery about nature.
responses.response: In round 1 I asked whether the many-atom lattice is a conceptual advance over single-ion clocks, and your picture of one trapping wavelength that shifts both levels equally together with Kroll's account has convinced me. I also thank you for the point that calculations underlie the claim of 1e-18, since a systematic uncertainty at that level is only credible when theory and several independent measurements agree. On your alternatives, I still rank B014 and B015 behind B005 for the reasons I gave in round 1, but I take your warning that a prize built only on measurement may look thin to some colleagues, so I want to keep the citation focused on the invention.

responses.point: He asks whether a two-part prize pairing B005 with a subset of Halzen, Karle and Spiering would be acceptable, and he calls the omitted names unfair, while accepting that the clock is cleanly attributed and well reproduced.
responses.response: I would not support pairing B005 with a subset of the IceCube names. The three-name cap forces that choice, and cutting a collaboration-scale discovery to one or two names would make the attribution worse than the contested but bounded two-name case for B005. If outside experts later give a firm view of who in IceCube carries the decisive credit, I would reconsider it in a future year. For this year I think a single, well-bounded part is the better outcome, and I would not add a second part only to fill the prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice is a conceptual step beyond the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which is my current view but rests on the mechanism and not on the priority record.

Priority chronology between Katori's 2001-2003 proposal, the first strontium lattice-clock measurements and the contributions of Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and Derevianko; outside expert checks of the primary papers would be needed.
Whether the formal redefinition of the SI second should be awaited; I think not, but I cannot rule out that members read the timing differently.
If a second part were wanted, whether B014 could be bounded in credit (Cao, Dean, Efetov and others) and whether the pairing mechanism needs to be settled first.
I have not independently verified accuracy figures and rely on recollection and my colleagues' statements.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict for B005 (Katori, Ye): I have no recorded personal or institutional tie to either laureate. I ranked B043 (Car-Parrinello) first at the opening, and such methods belong to my own computational field, but B043 is not in my final configuration and I have no personal tie to Car or Parrinello. I have no recorded connection to the B014, B015 or B020 candidates either.
